newsitem.title: SUDAN: Thousands of Sudan villagers flee fighting.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Sudan villagers flee fighting.

text.p: By camel caravan or barefoot through the bush, hundreds of villagers are abandoning their homes in southern Sudan to escape the war with rebels.
Shaded by a grass canopy, women in tribal robes cradled listless babies in the southern village of Kirma, where authorities have erected a makeshift camp for displace people.
Bags of clothes hung from the matchstick limbs of little boys, their bellies distended, as they played in the dirt.
"We came because of Habasha," said one little boy, using the Arabic word for Ethiopia, which Sudan says is behind the fighting against the Khartoum government.
"We hear they kill people," he added.
Sudan says Eritrea is also fighting for the rebels but both countries deny they have taken part in any fighting.

Standing at the threshold of a grass hut, Asha Hamed shyly drew the corners of her bright orange robe across her mouth and said she and her family fled Wad al-Mahi village further south because they were afraid of the war.
The village is one of 23 where up to 35,000 people have already left their homes or were expected to, Blue Nile provincial governor Ali Maqit told Reuters.
Much of the fighting has take place in the east and south of the province as rebels are threatening to take a strategic dam near Damazin town, about 40 km (25 miles) north of Kirma.
The opposition fighters have already taken the two small towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan, and officials said three other villages have also fallen.
"We are erecting camps in Kirma to eventually hold up to 20,000 people who left because of the fighting," Maqit said. "The rest have gone north or found families in other villages."
He said that there were about 3,000 people already at Kirma, about 570 km (360 miles) south of Khartoum. He did not give any population figures for the 23 villages.

The Swiss-based charity Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said in a report this month that Sudanese government forces had "bombed and torched" villages across the Blue Nile area near the Ethiopian border.
It said at least 50,000 people had been forced to flee from their homes and that some were living in makeshift shelters or out in the open.
Blue Nile state official Bubakr Jabr Kablo said in Damazin that he was not aware of the CSI report, but that the villagers fled after the army attacked rebels and Ethiopians in southern villages.

"There were some attacks in these villages and this displaced some of our people from their villages near Wad al-Mahi and some other places, including the village of Um Darfa near the Ethiopian border," he added.
The army and People's Defence Forces have set up a forward position in Wadi al-Mahi, about 35 km (22 miles) south of Kirma.
Maqit said people were making their own way to Kirma camp or were going in trucks sent by local authorities to fetch them.
Travellers heading south of Kirma, a trip which takes hours on a winding dirt road, saw several hundred people heading north from Wadi al-Mahi.
But it was difficult to gauge the extent of any migration along the isolated road, which passes through plains of grass and thorny trees and remote reed huts dotting gentle hills.
Villagers hunting with bow and arrow emerged suddenly from the trees onto the narrow road, pausing to wave wide-eyed at passing vehicles.
But others were clearly moving house. Villagers were perched on top of heavy trucks packed with furniture and food and suitcases that trundled along the dirt road.
One man said he walked five days to reach Kirma. Another said: "We have no food, no water. I have three children. What am I going to do?"
